item.title: Supporting App for CUBE - v0.7.1 [Version Update]
item.description:

Release Notes:
* **Important** - fixed the ciscoguid field, which rested on a bad assumption about zero padding and so could never match the equivalent CUCM value. Depending on the era of the data this affected anywhere from a few percent of records to all of them. * **Important** - fixed a bug whereby roughly one call in sixteen had no call\_reference\_id extracted, for the same reason. Those calls were silently absent from the CUBE to CUCM call rollup. * call\_reference\_id and ciscoguid are now extracted separately, so a malformed guid no longer takes call\_reference\_id out with it. * Added two diagnostic fields, ciscoguid\_source and ciscoguid\_source\_shape, recording where a guid came from and what the source field held when none came out. * Fixed the search-time duration fallback for CUBE data indexed before you upgraded TA\_cube. In 0.7.0 it silently produced nothing, so cube\_duration, duration\_total, duration\_in\_minutes and dateTimeDisconnect were empty on that data. Data indexed by the current TA was never affected. * Added an "All fields" panel to the call\_detail view for cube calls so the user can page through every value of every field. A search filter can filter against both names and values. * Added a "call quality stats" panel to the call\_detail view for cube calls. * The rows in the two "Other calls to/from" panels on the call\_detail view for cube calls are now clickable, and take you to that call. Those panels also show a progress indicator while their searches run. * The call\_detail view for cube calls no longer requires the Cisco CDR app to be installed alongside this one. It referenced two search macros, a stylesheet, a pattern and a custom behavior that only that app shipped. * The vg\_info\_types, vg\_q931\_cause\_codes and vg\_codec\_type\_rates lookups now carry this release's version in their filenames. Their contents changed in 0.7.0 without that rename, which on a search head cluster meant the deployer will not have pushed those changes to the peers. * Renamed the automatic lookup key LOOKUP-causeCode to LOOKUP-cubeCauseCode, matching the same rename in the Cisco CDR app. The old name was also used by that app for an unrelated CUCM lookup, which made errors naming it ambiguous.


Description:

These two apps are furthermore designed to work with Sideview's commercial "Cisco CDR Reporting and Analytics" app. When all three components are present and deployed to the right tiers, users can navigate, troubleshoot and build ad-hoc charts and reports around your CUBE data, within the the Cisco CDR app's complex user interfaces.

item.title: Cisco CDR Reporting and Analytics - v8.4.5 [Version Update]
item.description:
Platform: Splunk


Release Notes:
* **Important** — all CVP configuration has moved out of this app. If you index CVP logs, install the new TA\_​cisco\_​cvp add-on on your forwarders and indexers, and SA\_​cisco\_​ucce on your search heads. Without both, the cvp and cvp\_​log sourcetypes lose their fields. * **Important** — the ciscoguid field for CUCM CDR no longer emits empty strings, nor the SCCP and other non-guid call references that share the ProtocolCallRef columns. On clusters with a lot of phone-to-phone calling those were a large share of legs, and were being rolled up across sourcetypes as though they were guids. * **Important** — fixed the ciscoguid field for CUBE data, which rested on a bad assumption about zero padding and so could never match the equivalent CUCM value. Depending on the era of the data this affected anywhere from a few percent of records to all of them. * Fixed a bug whereby roughly one CUBE call in sixteen had no call\_​reference\_​id extracted, again due to an erroneous assumption about padding. Those calls were silently absent from the CUBE to CUCM call rollup. * Added two diagnostic fields, ciscoguid\_​source and ciscoguid\_​source\_​shape, on every sourcetype that produces a ciscoguid. They record where the value came from, and what the source field held when no value came out. * Added a search macro, get\_​ciscoguid\_​family, which decodes a guid into its encoding family and the identity of the box that minted it. * Added ciscoguid to fields.conf with INDEXED\_VALUE \= false. Without it, a search for ciscoguid\=\ matched nothing on the sourcetypes where we calculate the value rather than read it verbatim. * Added two hidden diagnostic pages, guid\_​rollup and guid\_​diagnostics, reachable by URL only. The second displays counts and shapes only — no guids, party numbers or addresses — so it is safe to screenshot and send to us. * Fixed an off-by-one in the build\_​call\_​guid\_​words transform, which truncated the first guid word. Nothing references it, so this affects only installations that enabled it locally. * Fixed the search-time duration fallback for CUBE data indexed before you upgraded your TA. In 8.4.4 it silently produced nothing, so cube\_​duration, duration\_​total, duration\_​in\_​minutes and dateTimeDisconnect were empty on that data. Data indexed by the current TA was never affected. * Fixed the second video channel’s codec lookup which now writes destVideoCodec\_​Channel2 and origVideoCodec\_Channel2. * The ring\_​time field is now deprecated in favour of seconds\_​until\_​answered, which measures the same interval without claiming the time was spent ringing — it can just as easily be announcement audio. ring\_​time was also empty on every call that never connected, the one case that branch of it exists for, and that is fixed. * The field gallery and the vg\_​info\_​types, vg\_​q931\_​cause\_​codes and vg\_​codec\_​type\_​rates lookups now carry this release’s version in their filenames. Their contents changed in 8.4.3 and 8.4.4 without that rename, which on a search head cluster meant the deployer never pushed the new data to the peers. * Renamed the automatic lookup keys LOOKUP-causeCode to LOOKUP-cucmCauseCode on cucm\_​cdr and LOOKUP-cubeCauseCode on cube\_​cdr. One name meant two different lookups, and Splunk’s ​“Could not load lookup” error prints only the key, so the two could not be told apart.


Description:
This commercial app is available as a 60 day trial and is compatible with both Splunk Enterprise and Splunk Cloud. The app gives your team greatly increased visibility, monitoring, and reporting functionality around Cisco Unified Communications (aka CUCM / CallManager), whether you're a small organization with a hundred phones or one of the largest companies in the world. Whether troubleshooting individual calls or building high level reporting, it helps you visualize and understand in all areas: agents, users, and huntgroups; concurrency and utilization; call flow; call quality; call volume; devices; failed calls; locations and sites; and audits and compliance. Your team can trust it as their day-to-day tool for navigating call data from your Cisco CallManager deployment, and it can also become their main tool for building custom reports, alerts and dashboards around that data. Note that this isn't a package of content, but more a tank that allows you to drive around in your data. You won’t find a leftnav full of canned CDR reports to click on (that "don't quite fit"). Description:
MITRE ATLAS is the adversarial threat matrix for AI/ML systems — the AI equivalent of MITRE ATT&CK. As organizations deploy LLMs, RAG pipelines, and ML APIs into production, they create an attack surface that most Splunk deployments have zero detection coverage for. This app provides 10 detection rules for AI and LLM threats — 9 mapped to specific MITRE ATLAS technique IDs, plus 1 vendor-defined rule where no canonical ATLAS technique covers the detection concept. Each rule is a Splunk saved search that monitors your AI/LLM logs for known attack patterns including prompt injection, jailbreak attempts, data exfiltration via inference APIs, training data poisoning, model reconnaissance, and AI abuse. The app includes a guided Setup dashboard that auto-discovers AI/LLM data in your environment, validates required fields, and shows which rules your data supports. A Configuration Guide provides platform-specific instructions for 12 LLM providers including LiteLLM, Azure OpenAI, AWS Bedrock, OpenAI, GCP Vertex AI, Kong AI Gateway, Portkey, Helicone, Cloudflare AI Gateway, Anthropic, self-hosted models (Ollama, vLLM, TGI), and custom API gateways. Rules are organized into two tiers: Tier 1 (Operational) — works with standard telemetry: token counts, API call volumes, storage access logs. Available from most platforms with default logging. Tier 2 (Content Inspection) — requires actual prompt/response text in log events. Requires explicit opt-in on all major platforms. The Configuration Guide explains how to enable this for each provider. Detection Coverage: AML.T0051.000 Direct Prompt Injection (Tier 2) AML.T0051.001 Indirect Prompt Injection via Retrieved Content (Tier 2) AML.T0054 LLM Jailbreak (Tier 2) AML.T0024 Exfiltration via AI Inference API (Tier 1) AML.T0020 Training Data Poisoning (Tier 1) GIC-VD-001 AI-Enabled Bulk Content Generation — vendor-defined, no canonical MITRE ATLAS technique covers this concept (Tier 1) AML.T0048 External Harms (Tier 1) AML.T0012 Valid Accounts (Tier 1) AML.T0014 Discover AI Model Family (Tier 2) AML.T0007 Discover AI Artifacts (Tier 1) All rules ship disabled by default. No Python scripts, no external dependencies — pure SPL and CSV lookups. Detection results are written to the summary index for fast dashboard rendering. Built by a Splunk Enterprise Architect with 10+ years of hands-on experience. This app is a standalone community release from GIC Engineering Consultants. Looking for broader AI/LLM threat coverage alongside SBOM security and CVE correlation? I also published a Supply Chain & AI Threat Intelligence Platform (SCIP) app: splunkbase.splunk.com/app/8814. Its free tier includes 10 comparable AI/agentic threat rules (9 MITRE ATLAS-mapped) at no cost. Paid tiers include 66 AI/agentic threat rules (57 MITRE ATLAS-mapped), plus additional capabilities.

item.title: Language Entropy - v1.0.3 [New App Release]
item.description:
Platform: Splunk


Short Description:
Scores text fields against bigram language models to detect strings atypical for a language — random names, DGA domains, hashes, and other machine-generated sequences.


Description:
The Apius Language Entropy app measures how well any string matches the character patterns of a given language. Its custom search command computes bigram cross-entropy against trained language models: strings built from natural, language-typical character sequences receive low scores, while random-looking or machine-generated strings — hashes, tokens, encoded payloads, algorithmically generated names — stand out with high scores. Unlike plain Shannon entropy, which only measures character distribution within a string, cross-entropy scoring evaluates strings against real language statistics, reliably separating genuine words from random sequences built from the same characters. Scoring works with any language: the app ships with a Polish (default) and English bigram models and lets you build and upload models for other languages from simple frequency files through its web interface. Scoring the same field against multiple models also reveals which language a string most likely belongs to. Typical applications include security use cases such as detecting DGA domains, DNS tunneling, and C2 traffic hiding behind random-looking names, as well as broader data-quality and anomaly-detection scenarios: spotting machine-generated identifiers where human-given names are expected, flagging encoded or obfuscated content in logs, and filtering garbage values in text fields. The app includes the entropy streaming search command (usable in any SPL pipeline), a model-management page for converting bigram frequency files into ready-to-use probability models, and an interactive Entropy Lab for scoring individual strings or batch files, tuning thresholds with per-model summary statistics, and exporting results to CSV.

item.description:
Platform: Splunk


Release Notes:
# Adjutant AI (formerly AI Workbench) — Release notes What's new, improved, and fixed in each release, in plain language. This is the **customer-facing** summary used for the Splunkbase release-notes section; the full technical changelog lives in the project's detailed release notes. **Last updated:** 2026-08-05 > **About version numbers.** Releases once numbered 0.10–0.13 were renumbered to > 1.0–1.3 to reflect production maturity — no behaviour changed. The current release is > **2.2.1** — a maintenance release on top of **2.2.0**'s **Explain a SPL search**, and **2.1.0**'s **Fraud capability** and the **2.0 line** (the deterministic **ITSI Root > Cause Analysis** engine, **resource-consumption monitoring**, and **2.0.7**'s durable memory, > Scheduled Ask and governed integrations), which in turn built on > **1.8.5** (the **CIM Coverage Audit**), **1.8.4** (async playbook execution over MCP > plus the **Outcome Ledger** executive/audit dashboard), **1.8.3** > (a security‑hardening release: OWASP + dependency + anti‑ransomware audit), **1.8.2** (Splunk > Edge Processor data‑quality awareness and keyless Azure OpenAI authentication), **1.8.1** > (support‑diagnosis fixes) and **1.8.0** (agent telemetry & OCSF export, content packs, > all‑tiers data‑quality checks, Splunk 10.x readiness, Dashboard Studio version‑awareness). The > **1.7.0** ServiceNow integration and the **1.5.0 "Data Foundation & MCP OAuth"** themes are > included below. --- ## 2.2.1 "Proven" A maintenance release, and every item in it came from running 2.2.0 against a real estate rather than from reading the code. One new capability came along with the fixes. ### Fraud rings your risk threshold cannot see (Enterprise, fraud-analytics) Risk-based alerting adds up one entity's score across many events. A fraud ring is the opposite shape: many entities sharing one thing. Because those are different questions, no amount of threshold tuning finds a ring. Seventeen mule accounts each earning fifteen points against a threshold of forty are seventeen well-behaved customers, since the risk was split seventeen ways and no single account ever crossed. Lower the threshold and you get seventeen false positives, not one ring. This release adds the query that asks the other question: group by the shared attribute instead of by the account. Nothing new has to be collected, because fraud risk rules have always recorded the linking attribute alongside the score. It simply was never read back this way. It is rarity-weighted, which matters more than it sounds. Ask only "what is shared" and the answer is always the corporate proxy that everybody sits behind. Shared attributes are ranked the same way the Fraud Ring Mapper ranks them, so a shared password hash and a shared IP are never treated as equal evidence, and values that are simply infrastructure are shown separately rather than quietly removed — a short list should not be mistaken for a clean estate. It is also honest about one thing it cannot know. It counts accounts that some rule already scored, which is not the same as how many accounts exist that share the value. So it hands you the search that settles it against your real data, and until you run that, it labels its own confidence as provisional instead of guessing. If you cannot name a starting account, the Fraud Ring Mapper will now find candidates for you before it starts walking. ### Fixed - **Money laundering was graded ready on two weeks of data.** Structuring is a run of individually unremarkable deposits and layering is a graph, so neither is visible in a short window however complete the feed is. Our own use case catalogue has always said to grade retention as well as fields; the grader printed that note and never acted on it. History is now graded, and a use case whose data does not go back far enough is capped at partial with the shortfall named. It is worth separating from other gaps, because it is the one you close with a retention policy rather than an onboarding project. On our demo estate this moved money laundering from ready to partial. - **Every ServiceNow tool call failed** with an internal error reference and no explanation. A tenant lookup returned a dictionary and the calling code expected a pair. - **The fraud readiness dashboard.** Four defects, found by running it rather than reading it. The readiness lookup was private to our own app, so when a dashboard was generated into a customer app the summary panel could not resolve it and rendered empty — which reads as "nothing has been graded" rather than "you cannot see it from here". The audit's own verdicts were being re-graded on the way to the screen, so nine computed verdicts became eight different ones. The coverage audit could not reach the dashboard builder at all, so nothing enforced that a panel must return data before it goes on the glass, and an empty panel on a fraud dashboard is read as "nothing wrong". And no fraud dashboard mentioned data quality: no ingestion check, no TrackMe, no Cribl or Edge Processor. A readiness grade computed over a feed that is arriving late or half delivered is a confident answer about the wrong data, and it fails towards "you are ready". That panel is now mandatory and appears even when everything is clean, because "we checked and it is healthy" is a finding. - **Asking for a readiness audit in plain English now reaches the readiness audit.** The question our own demo guide tells people to ask did not route to the playbook it names. - **Fraud verdict columns are coloured.** Ready, partial and blocked — and the feed inventory's present and absent — were missing from the status colour map, so those columns could only be coloured by hand and often were not. - **A dashboard opened from a finished session sat on "Loading..."** until you refreshed the tab. The new tab was sharing a browser process with a page that was still busy, so it never got a chance to start. - **The dashboard builder could refuse a fix it gave no way to make.** A publish refusal asked for a base search to be amended, and nothing could amend one, so the assistant looped between rebuilding and hand-editing. There is now a tool for it. - **The write-confirmation prompt asked about writes that could not succeed.** You were approving changes that validation then refused anyway. Validation now runs first, so the prompt only appears for writes that can actually happen. - **Token and cost accounting missed cached tokens.** With prompt caching the provider reports only the uncached part of the input, so an agentic run showed a few thousand tokens next to a cost that looked impossible. Cached tokens are now recorded, priced and shown. This affected what we reported, never what you were charged. - **Test Connection for Azure could only ever time out on a broken network.** Its own retries outlasted the window Splunk Web allows, so you got a bare 504 instead of the staged diagnostic. It now finishes inside the window and tells you which stage failed. ### Improved - **History groups by conversation.** A playbook run and its follow-up replies were listed as separate entries. They are now one entry with the turns nested inside and a combined cost. - **Large tool results no longer inflate every later call.** A stateless chat API re-sends the whole conversation on each tool round-trip, so one oversized result was paid for repeatedly. Results are now bounded before they enter the conversation. --- ## 2.2.0 "Explain" ### Explain a SPL search — free on every tier Point it at a search and get back an explanation you keep. Paste the SPL, name a saved search, or give it a dashboard and let it explain every panel. You get a private dashboard and a private saved search holding the same search fully commented, using native SPL comments so the commented copy is still a real, runnable search rather than a printout. This is on **every tier, including the free one**. Reading somebody else's search is the first thing a new Splunk user needs and the last thing they should have to pay for. **It explains what the search does here, not what the commands mean in general.** Your macros are expanded to their real definitions. `tag=web` is resolved to the eventtypes it actually selects on your system. Lookups are shown with their real columns. Command behaviour comes from your own installation's grammar, so an app-contributed command is described correctly. **And it runs the thing.** The pipeline is split at up to four points and each piece is executed over your sample window, so the walkthrough says "the base search returns 4,812 events with 14 extracted fields; after `stats count by host, status` that becomes 37 rows with 3 fields" using your real names and numbers. A field the SPL references that never appears in the results is flagged — the most common silent SPL bug, and one no text-only explainer can see. A search that returns nothing is bracketed to the stage where it broke. Nothing it could not verify is presented as if it were. Verified and unverified statements are never mixed together quietly. ### "Explain this" is usually "why did this stop working" Those two questions arrive in the same sentence, and reading SPL cannot tell them apart: a search whose data stopped arriving looks exactly like a search that was always wrong. So every run takes a feed verdict for the indexes involved, whether or not the search looked healthy. A source that stopped reporting half its hosts, or is arriving four hours late, still returns rows and still looks right — that is precisely when a check is worth having. When something does look off it goes further: ingestion parsing errors, Cribl Stream and Edge Processor if they front your indexers, and the CIM layer, where a perfectly written search returns nothing because acceleration has not backfilled or the index is not in the data model's allowlist. All of that is available on every tier. The per-field CIM audit still needs Professional, and when it is not available the dashboard says so in place, naming what that audit would have told you. ### Fixed - **CIM Coverage Audit acceleration check.** Since 1.8.5 it reported "not visible to the data model" for every source on every estate, because of how it referenced the sourcetype field in `tstats`. It now reports the real counts. If you have run a CIM audit before and were told acceleration could not see your data, run it again. - **Generated dashboards.** Splunk rejects malformed markup with the single unhelpful phrase "Invalid XML."; the app now says what is actually wrong and repairs the common cases itself. Panels bound to a shared base search are checked for the field-pruning trap that makes a panel render empty, or show a wrong number, while the same search works fine when opened in Search. --- ## 2.1.0 "Fraud" Splunk's own App for Fraud Analytics reaches end of life on 1 May 2027, and it is not alone: the App for Anomaly Detection retired in 2025, standalone UBA ends in January 2027, and the App for Behavioral Profiling froze at Splunk 9.4. Four packaged analytics apps retiring on one path, and their customers have no answer today. This release is that answer. - **Find out what your data can actually support, in about a minute.** The Fraud Data Coverage Audit reads your real events and tells you which fraud use cases you can run today, which are partial and why, and which are blocked with the feed that is missing named. It works out which of your sources is which by looking at what they CONTAIN, not what they are called, because real sourcetypes never match the documentation. Today this answer takes a workshop and three weeks of a consultant. - **The check nobody else makes.** It measures whether your entity keys actually survive from one feed to the next. Ring detection is the payoff use case and it is the one most often declared ready on the strength of the fields being present, then failing because an account or device cannot be followed across the boundary. It also tells you when a feed carries every field perfectly but only knows about a fraction of your customers, which is a different problem with a different fix. - **Count actors, not accounts.** One person can open many accounts using the fact that Gmail ignores dots, and to your signup system they look like many different people. Adjutant knows to collapse those, and knows NOT to do it for other providers, where merging two customers would invent a fraud ring that does not exist. When it links entities it always shows you how rare the shared attribute is, because a shared IP address means nothing behind a mobile network and a great deal on a home line. - **Scoring that fits where you already are.** If you run Enterprise Security, everything goes into your existing risk framework and nothing parallel is built. If you do not, it uses the same field names anyway, so the day you buy ES you change a destination rather than rewrite your detections. - **Behavioural profiling that outlives the app it replaces.** Describe the behaviour in a sentence and get a working indicator, anomaly rule and ranked entity list. It compares an entity against its own history, or against its peer group, which the retiring app could not do. It also watches for a feed dying behind a profile: when that happens the scores simply fade, and fading looks exactly like everyone behaving better. - **Nothing here needs those retiring apps.** Every playbook, tool and piece of knowledge works on a plain Splunk estate. What we took from the retiring apps is their METHOD, not a dependency on them: the risk-contribution model, the behavioural profiling pattern, the entity pivots and the fraud use case catalogue are all reimplemented here and improved. If you do still run either app, importers can lift what you built into the native form, but that is a convenience rather than the point. - **The fraud patterns it now knows.** Signup fraud (many accounts sharing an email, IP, phone, password or bank account), account takeover (brute force against credential stuffing, one address against many accounts, impossible travel, and the profile-change-then-money-movement chain), money laundering (funds converging then dispersing, amounts kept just under a reporting threshold, sanctioned-country exposure), and two narrow verticals in unemployment-insurance claims and controlled-substance diversion. All of it reworded into our own framing, with nothing copied from Splunk's documentation. - **Eight playbooks**, including triage for both public sector claims and financial fraud. Both start by checking the data is actually flowing before offering any verdict, because a quiet fraud queue is either good news or a dead feed, and you should know which. Fraud features need Splunk Enterprise and the fraud licence feature. Where either is missing they stay visible and explain what is needed rather than disappearing. The demonstration dataset has no licence requirement at all, so a trial environment always works. One thing said plainly: Adjutant AI is not a fraud detection engine and does not try to be. It will not decline a card payment in a hundred milliseconds; that is what the dedicated engines are for. It is the layer above them that finds what they miss across channels, connects the entities they cannot, and turns three weeks of investigation into an afternoon with a trail you can hand to an auditor. ## 2.0.7 "Memory, Scheduled Ask & Integrations" Adjutant AI gains a durable memory, a scheduled/unattended surface, and a governed data-integration subsystem — so it stops re-asking, can run on a clock, and can sync a system of record into Splunk under a contract two humans have reviewed. - **Memory — it stops re-asking.** A small, durable, per-tenant memory: **learned facts** (the index a report uses, what "the Cribl search" means for a team) captured the moment they're learned, and **integration watermarks**. Two new Knowledge tabs — **Learned Knowledge** (a confirm queue; promote a fact to the whole Org) and **Integration State** (force a watermark to replay or skip). Unattended runs use **confirmed facts only**; a captured-but-unconfirmed fact can't silently steer a run that writes to a target. Description:
Adjutant AI (formerly AI Workbench) is a generative workspace for Splunk — not a chatbot bolted onto search, but a real workbench where you investigate, analyse and build with tools that understand Splunk. It is a host shell: it has no use-cases of its own, deriving everything from the Splunk app a user opens it from and their roles. Where a generic MCP-only assistant talks to Splunk through one broad door, Adjutant AI ships fine-grained, Splunk-aware tools across Core, Enterprise Security, ITSI, TrackMe, ServiceNow and the AI Toolkit, each scoped to one job and run under your existing Splunk ACLs. Extend it with HTTP tools or any MCP server. New in 2.1 — a fraud capability that starts by telling you what you cannot yet detect. Entity resolution runs before scoring, because risk accumulates per entity. Generated rules are weighted contributions with readable reasons, emitted into Enterprise Security's risk framework where it exists and into RBA's own field vocabulary where it does not. Nothing generated is ever enabled or scheduled. New in 2.0 — ITSI Root Cause Analysis with no LLM in the answer. It walks your real dependency graph, verifies the data behind every KPI, scores the evidence transparently, then lets an LLM narrate. The same evidence always gives the same answer. Plus durable memory, scheduled playbooks, governed integrations, and per-tenant resource-consumption reporting. Your SOC can watch the agent: LLM calls, tool and ServiceNow calls, config changes, unattended verdicts and policy refusals emitted as OCSF events to an index Enterprise Security already watches. On-prem, no cloud egress, off by default. Bring your own LLM: Anthropic, OpenAI, Azure OpenAI, Groq, Gemini, Bedrock, Ollama (fully offline) or OpenRouter — server-side, so keys never leave the search head. Multi-tenant by design. Description:

When a data source goes silent — whether from a misconfigured forwarder, a failed log shipper, or a broken integration — Data Heartbeat detects the gap and alerts you before the silence becomes a blind spot. Every monitored source type has a configurable threshold, measured in minutes. When no data arrives within that window, the app flags the source type and fires your chosen alert action: Slack, Microsoft Teams, a generic webhook, or email via Splunk's built-in SMTP relay. Key features: • Monitor dashboard — a live status table showing every tracked source type, the minutes since its last event, its threshold, and its importance level, with color-coded severity (green, yellow, red, and critical). • Per-row alert actions — each source type can use its own notification target, independent of the global default. • Auto Discovery — a nightly scan that surfaces new source types appearing in your environment and queues them for review. • Importance tagging — mark business-critical sources as High, Medium, or Low importance. When a high-importance source goes silent, the app raises a red-alert banner. • Settings page — configure global defaults (threshold, alert action, and notification target), enable or disable the monitoring pipeline, and test alert actions without waiting for a real outage. • Audit log — a full history of every configuration change, with timestamps and user attribution. • No index footprint — all configuration is stored in KV Store, so no custom indexes are required. Data Heartbeat is compatible with Splunk Enterprise 8.2+, Splunk Cloud Classic, and Splunk Cloud Victoria.

item.title: CCX Add-on for AWS Products - v1.2.9 [Version Update]
item.description:
Platform: Splunk


Release Notes:
Updated Support For AWS Security Hub Findings logs via EventBridge


Description:
About Us: CyberCX is Australia’s greatest force of cyber security experts. Our highly skilled professional services team operates a 24x7 on-shore security operations centre (SOC) servicing corporate and public sector organisations across Australia and New Zealand, specialising in Security Operations services leveraging Splunk. Description: CCX Security Operations has taken it upon ourselves to develop a CCX Add-on for AWS Products to provide further CIM compliance coverage not only for logs ingested via 'Splunk Add-on for AWS'. This TA was built using a large dataset and endeavours to be the most CIM compliant comprehensive field extraction for AWS various products listed. The Technical Addon is designed for ingest based on an SQS-Based S3 "Custom Data Type" via the Splunk Add-on for AWS or Syslog and is to be used on Search Heads. Listed products supported: - AWS Network Firewall - AWS Web Application Firewall - AWS S3 VPC Flow - AWS Macie - AWS API Gateway Access Logs - AWS Security Hub Custom (HEC|JSON) Features: - This TA currently supports logtypes tagged under the following CIM datamodels: Alert, Change, Network Traffic and Web.
